paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Thermal conduction is the spreading of heat within one material, or between materials that touch. In the hotter object, the molecules carry more kinetic energy, and spreading among the molecules shares it out until the energy is even throughout. Heat flows on its own from hotter to colder. A stove's hot plate warming the bottom of a saucepan is conduction at work. Unless something keeps feeding energy in, temperature differences fade and the objects approach thermal equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: One of three ways heat moves
paragraphs.text: Conduction is heat moving by physical contact, while the matter itself stays still on a large scale. Convection is heat carried by a fluid that moves, as in a forced-air furnace or in weather. Radiation is heat carried by infrared, visible light or other electromagnetic radiation. The Sun warming the Earth is an obvious case, and the heat given off by a human body is a less obvious one.

paragraphs.heading: Solids, liquids and gases
paragraphs.text: Conduction is the main way heat moves through solids. Strong forces between their molecules let particle vibrations pass along easily. Liquids have weaker forces and more room between particles, so vibrations travel less well. Gases have even more room, so their particles collide only rarely. That is why liquids and gases are poor conductors of heat.

paragraphs.heading: Why metals conduct well
paragraphs.text: Metals such as copper, platinum and gold are usually good conductors. Their metallic bonds have free-moving electrons that pass thermal energy along quickly, so this electron fluid carries heat through the metal. In insulators, by contrast, heat is carried almost entirely by vibrations called phonons. Electrons also carry electric current through conducting solids, and in most metals the heat and electrical conductivities stand in roughly the same ratio. Copper, a good electrical conductor, also conducts heat well.

paragraphs.heading: Putting a number on it
paragraphs.text: Engineers describe how easily a material conducts with its thermal conductivity, written k. It is defined by how much heat passes, in a given time, through a given thickness and area because of a temperature difference. Its value depends mainly on the material's phase, temperature, density and molecular bonding.

paragraphs.heading: A bar in steady state
paragraphs.text: When the temperature difference driving conduction stays constant, an object settles after a while into steady-state conduction, where its pattern of temperatures stops changing. In that state, as much heat enters each region as leaves it. Picture a bar that is hot at one end and cold at the other. Once it is steady, the temperatures along it no longer shift with time, and if nothing inside the bar produces heat, the temperature changes in a straight line from end to end.
